a4c6813f24.q: Why does a 6% cap rate $2 million all-cash deal generate more year-one cash flow than a 7% cap rate $6 million deal with 65% leverage?
a4c6813f24.a: When you have positive leverage, you typically need 150 to 200 basis points of leverage spread between your going-in cap rate and your debt cost. In the current interest rate environment, a 7% cap rate deal with traditional 65% LTV financing at 7.25% or higher creates a situation where you're paying the bank more than you're generating in cash flow, whereas an all-cash deal at 6% generates positive cash flow immediately.
a4c6813f24.e: Beyond the Spreadsheet: What Makes a CRE Deal Worth Funding

fb4b6aa648.q: What minimum yield on cost do large institutional capital groups require before even considering a commercial real estate deal today?
fb4b6aa648.a: Large institutional groups, many of them industry agnostic, are looking for at least a minimum yield on cost of nine, just even to look at the deal. This is one of the key metrics investors are using to filter opportunities in the current market environment.
fb4b6aa648.e: Beyond the Spreadsheet: What Makes a CRE Deal Worth Funding

8c84943883.q: How does the current market differ from the Great Financial Crisis in terms of asset fundamentals and employment?
8c84943883.a: During the GFC in late 2007-2009, the music stopped and you had an unemployment crisis, but you were seeing performing assets available at deep discounts. Today, you have full employment and performing assets, but you're seeing equity erosion instead. The key difference is that today you have a robust economy with high inflation—more stagflation than a financial crisis—whereas the GFC was primarily a financial engineering repricing event.

8cfde586c1.q: What validation process should real estate operators complete before pitching a deal to capital investors?
8cfde586c1.a: Operators should validate deal assumptions as much as possible in advance before pitching to investors, rather than just putting out an LOI and filling in spreadsheet numbers afterward. If you're an established operator with proven internal metrics, that's one thing, but if you're entering a new market or trying a new strategy, you have to go validate those numbers upfront. This upfront work demonstrates to investors the type of operator you are and that your numbers are credible, not just desktop projections.
8cfde586c1.e: Beyond the Spreadsheet: What Makes a CRE Deal Worth Funding

fbaa61c3f2.q: What operational details do spreadsheets typically miss when underwriting commercial real estate assets?
fbaa61c3f2.a: Spreadsheets often miss the business model of the previous operator and their cost structure. For example, if a previous owner was a self-managing mom-and-pop operation with low overhead, but you need to hire third-party property management, your cost structure will be significantly higher from day one. Spreadsheets also miss whether tenants listed on the rent roll are actually occupying space, deferred maintenance issues, or phantom tenants that haven't been on-site for months.
fbaa61c3f2.e: Beyond the Spreadsheet: What Makes a CRE Deal Worth Funding

b06d57083e.q: How should real estate investors determine their competitive edge when underwriting deals?
b06d57083e.a: Investors need to understand what Damon calls your eternal edge—what makes you different in the marketplace. You have to know who you are, what your cost structure is, and what your skill sets are. Your underwriting should reflect that edge, and you should pitch to investors specifically how your operation is better than competitors because of how you operate differently, which allows you to squeeze out additional IRR points. If a deal doesn't align with your edge and cost structure, it's better to pass than chase deals that don't fit your profile.
